title: The Tamil Veda comes home
hookLine: pilgrims sing ten verses that say they're part of a thousand, and a teacher sets out to find the rest
carry: the tamil veda: holy words in the people's tongue
tomorrow: a dead teacher's fingers curl tight. what promise opens them?

cards: Ten verses, sung by pilgrims at the temple in Kumbakonam. A teacher named Nathamuni hears them and is moved. Then he hears the last verse say these ten are part of a thousand.
A thousand? He asks the pilgrims for the rest. They don't have them.
He asks everywhere. Nobody does. That, the Sri Vaishnava tradition says, is how a lost Tamil scripture began to come home.
Year three met its singer, Nammalvar, the silent boy under the tamarind who answered a riddle. Today, how his songs were nearly lost, and found.

teach.b: So Nathamuni goes to Tirukkurugur, Nammalvar's town, to the tamarind where the silent boy once sat. Nobody there has the thousand either.
But, tradition says, someone gives him a short hymn: the one Madhurakavi, Nammalvar's disciple, sang in praise of his teacher. Recite this, he's told.
He does, over and over, until Nammalvar appears to him and gives back the hymns. Nathamuni sets them to music and teaches them, and his line of teachers would later reach Ramanuja.
The key wasn't a library, but a disciple's song of love for his teacher. What came back is the Tiruvaymoli, longing set to verse. Sometimes Nammalvar sings as himself.
Sometimes he sings as a girl missing her beloved, sending birds as messengers to Vishnu. And sometimes the joy is so full that God and the singer seem to have swallowed each other.
Tradition calls this song the Tamil Veda. That's a big claim, said plainly: for Sri Vaishnavas, scripture isn't only Sanskrit.
A saint's song in the language people spoke at home is Veda too, and they speak of two Vedantas, Sanskrit and Tamil, read together.

how: Sri Vaishnavas chant Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temples and homes alongside the Sanskrit Veda, and remember Nathamuni as the teacher who recovered the hymns.

games.q: you're Nathamuni. you've heard ten beautiful verses that say they're part of a thousand, and nobody has the rest. what do you do?
o: go to Nammalvar's town and keep reciting his disciple's hymn.
games.why: tradition says he went to Tirukkurugur and recited Madhurakavi's hymn to Nammalvar until Nammalvar appeared and gave him all the hymns.

practice: Walk back through the Alvar days, one breath for each: the king who asked to be a step, Tiruppan's slow look from the feet up, Andal's girls at the door, three lamps in the rain, Periyalvar's many years, and ten verses that led to a thousand.
Don't weigh them; notice which one stays a moment longer, and rest there. If you pray, you can offer that moment to God.

wordCard.voice: The Alvar hymns. Today, Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli, lost and found again through a disciple's small hymn, which the tradition calls the Tamil Veda.

orig.note: Tamil: the name of Nammalvar's great hymn, which Sri Vaishnavas call the Tamil Veda.

carryVoice: Your line: the Tamil Veda, holy words in the people's tongue. One small hymn sung again and again, and a thousand came home. Until tomorrow.
